newsitem.title: UK: Defiant Major sticks to guns over Europe.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Major sticks to guns over Europe.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major rounded defiantly on his critics on Sunday and declared that he would not be "held to ransom" by party members opposed to closer links with Europe.
Major made clear he would not give in to blackmail by so-called "Eurosceptic" legislators who have threatened to make trouble now that his one-seat parliamentary majority has disappeared.

Despite his media image as a "grey man", Major's performance in a BBC television interview was reminiscent of his gamble 18 months ago when he called an election for the party leadership and defeated his anti-European challenger.
The Opposition Labour Party said the interview made clear that Major's problems were far from over.

"Mr Major has admitted for the first time that the Tory (Conservative) divisions are damaging the national interest and it is clear that the Conservatives are incapable of representing Britain's interests in Europe," said Labour finance spokesman Gordon Brown.
"The British people are not likely to trust a prime minister who does not have the trust of his own party."
A top Conservative anti-European, John Redwood, who challenged for the party leadership last year, urged Major not to compromise with the EU.
"I do hope the Prime Minister will...demand justice for us: common market, yes; common government, no," Redwood said.

Major had been expected to appeal for party unity at the end of a week that left the Conservatives, in the view of some commentators, damaged beyond repair as a result of their bitter divisions over Europe.
Instead, Major said he had no intention of giving in to those Conservative members of parliament he called "mavericks".
"We are not going to be held to ransom," he said. "If you think I am thinking of packing my bags and walking off, you are wholly wrong."
Major insisted there would be no change on his "wait-and-see" policy on British entry into a European single currency before the election -- which he said would be held not later than next May 1.
He defended his pro-European Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister), Kenneth Clarke, whom some anti-European MPs had demanded he sack.
But for the benefit of party "Eurosceptics" opposed to European integration, he also stressed Britain would not join a single currency if other countries "fudge" the economic criteria for entry.
Britain would, however, not abandon negotiations with its European partners.

"Whether we go into a single currency or whether we stay out of it, it is going to affect the UK in very significant ways. I believe it is in the national interest for the British government to be in there negotiating," Major said.
The latest opinion poll puts the opposition Labour Party 37 points ahead of Major's party, and next week bristles with traps for the Conservatives.

On Wednesday, the government starts a debate on Europe, with Eurosceptics in full cry. On Thursday, a by-election in the Labour stronghold of Barnsley in northern England is set to seal the government's status as a minority administration -- the first since 1979.
And on Friday, Major attends a European summit in Dublin where other leaders will push for more European integration leaving him isolated and exposed.
